A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TaTS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting and imputation experiments, frequency analyses, sensitivity studies, encoder comparisons, and efficiency measurements in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds alignment measurements, additional baseline evaluations, and text-corruption experiments in Tables 1 and 4–6.

M1.justification: TaTS retains text encoding, MLP projection, concatenation as auxiliary variables, and joint training with the existing time-series model. V2's imputation pseudocode documents an already evaluated application. TT-Wasserstein is an analytical metric and does not alter TaTS training or inference.

E1.justification: The nine Time-MMD domains and forecasting/imputation tasks remain unchanged. V2 adds corrupted input scenarios: time-series and text shuffling for alignment assessment, and text-shuffled forecasting on Climate, Security, and Traffic. No additional real-world dataset is evaluated.

E2.justification: V1 compares TaTS with numerical-only modeling and MM-TSFLib across nine backbones. V2 retains these comparisons and evaluates N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TCN, and ChatTime on Climate, Security, and Traffic in Table 5, substantially broadening the comparator families.

E3.justification: V2 introduces TT-Wasserstein measurement, original/shuffled distance ratios, and shuffling controls. New baseline protocols supply numerical/text embeddings to N-BEATS, N-HiTS, and TCN, and concatenated texts to zero-shot ChatTime. These supplement the retained forecasting horizons, imputation length, and hyperparameter settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of spectral alignment under shuffling, analysis relating alignment ratios to forecasting gains, and a direct text-corruption ablation (Tables 1, 4, and 6). These substantially extend investigation of the CTR rationale. Earlier sensitivity, encoder, efficiency, and single-feature analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Averaging across prediction lengths and the retained graphical reporting are unchanged. V2's explanation of Gaussian random forecasts concerns baseline construction, not uncertainty estimates for performance.

E6.justification: The matched original forecasting and imputation tables and figure results are unchanged. V2 adds alignment scores, alignment–gain comparisons, four-baseline results, and corruption outcomes. For example, Table 6 reports Climate MSE of 1.020 with aligned text and 1.147 with shuffled text; these compare input conditions within v2.

T1.justification: V2 adds the formal TT-Wasserstein definition and transport constraints in Equation 4. Appendix A also claims that the single-cosine arguments extend to mixtures through linear superposition. The two existing periodicity propositions and their derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: V2 makes quantifying CTR and alignment an explicit contribution and claims alignment strength can indicate TaTS's potential benefit. Its abstract and introduction also condition periodicity on data quality, narrowing v1's largely unqualified characterization. The central TaTS compatibility and performance claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 introduces PRH-based interpretation, connects alignment ratios with gains while qualifying sampling frequency and the Climate exception, and interprets shuffled text as noise. New Appendix B.2 identifies construction biases, unexamined neural mechanisms, text-quality dependence, and untested modalities/domains. V1 lacks this detailed limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, explicit imputation pseudocode, and input/inference details for the new baselines. Appendix E.1 clarifies how random forecasts use training-data statistics. Existing hyperparameters, hardware/software information, runtime and memory claims, and supplementary code/data descriptions are retained.

R1.justification: V2 newly grounds CTR in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and distinguishes TaTS from concurrent work in Appendix B.1, including CiK, Multi-modal Forecaster, and DualTime. It adds transport and baseline references and removes several peripheral graph/LLM references, substantially expanding research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are edited and compressed, and terminology and qualifications are refined. The single-feature example and forecasting algorithm move into reorganized appendices. Much of the existing method, proof, experimental, and related-work prose remains recognizable; the revision is not a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. V2 adds four tables, relocates and resizes existing displays, reformats algorithm presentation, and introduces red/blue highlighting in Table 2. All existing figure images are retained, although their placement, sizing, and captions change.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked a direct alignment-corruption control and detailed applicability limits; v2 supplies both, broadens baseline comparisons, and clarifies implementation. These improve credibility. The gain is limited because TT-Wasserstein's proposed predictive usefulness rests on descriptive comparisons, ChatTime has different supervision, and Appendix A's added linear-superposition argument is not justified for cosine similarity.
